title: Find the String with LCP
statement:
For a string `word` of length n made of lowercase English letters, its LCP matrix is the n x n grid whose cell `(i, j)` holds the length of the longest common prefix of two suffixes of `word`: the one starting at index `i` and the one starting at index `j` (indices are 0-based).

You receive an n x n matrix `lcp`. Return the lexicographically smallest string of lowercase letters whose LCP matrix equals `lcp` in every cell. If no such string exists, return the empty string `""`.
notes:
## Intuition

Any cell with `lcp[i][j] > 0` says `word[i]` and `word[j]` are the same letter, and a zero says they differ. So the matrix fixes which positions share a letter; only the names of the letters are free. To be smallest, give `'a'` to the group containing index 0, `'b'` to the group of the first index not yet named, and so on. That choice is forced, but the matrix may still be impossible, so finish by checking it against the string we built. Trying every string is hopeless (26^n), which is why the structure matters.

## Approach

1. Keep `word` as letter codes, all `-1` at first, and `next` as the next unused code.
2. Scan `i` from left to right. Skip indices that already have a code.
3. If 26 codes are already used, a 27th letter would be needed, so return `""`.
4. Give code `next` to every `j >= i` with `lcp[i][j] > 0`, then advance `next`.
5. Verify every cell from the bottom-right: equal letters need `lcp[i][j] = lcp[i + 1][j + 1] + 1` (or `1` on the last row or column), different letters need `0`. Any mismatch returns `""`.
6. Turn the codes into letters and return the string.

## Example 1, step by step

At `i = 0` the row `[4, 0, 2, 0]` puts code 0 on indices 0 and 2. At `i = 1` the row `[0, 3, 0, 1]` puts code 1 on indices 1 and 3. Indices 2 and 3 are already named, so `word` is `[0, 1, 0, 1]`. The check passes: for example `lcp[0][2] = lcp[1][3] + 1 = 2` and `lcp[3][3] = 1`. The answer is `"abab"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): the grouping pass and the check each visit every cell once.
- Space: O(n) for `word`; the check reads the input matrix instead of building a new one.

## Pitfalls

- Grouping alone is not enough: a symmetric-looking matrix can still have wrong lengths, such as a diagonal cell other than `n - i`.
- The check must run from the bottom-right so that `lcp[i + 1][j + 1]` is already known to be correct.
- More than 26 groups means no lowercase string exists, even when the matrix is otherwise consistent.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `word` | letter code chosen for each index, `-1` if none yet |
| `next` | the code the next new group receives |
| `i`, `j` | the cell being grouped or checked |
| `expected` | the value `lcp[i][j]` must have for the built string |

narration.5: Walk the indices from left to right so the earliest unnamed index always gets the smallest new letter.
narration.6: An index already named by an earlier row belongs to an existing group.

narration.10: No lowercase string can work, so give up.

narration.13: A positive common prefix means these two positions hold the same letter.
narration.14: Put index j into the new group.
narration.17: The next new group gets the following letter.
narration.19: Check every cell starting from the bottom-right corner, so the diagonal neighbour is already verified.
narration.22: Equal letters at i and j: the prefix extends the one starting one step later.
narration.23: Expect one more than lcp[i + 1][j + 1], or exactly 1 at the last row or column.
narration.25: The given value must match what the built string really produces.
narration.26: A single mismatch means no string fits the matrix.
narration.30: Every cell matched; turn the codes into letters and return the string.
